texts: The first High Definition (HD) broadcasts on TV began in the early 1980s, notably in France and Japan. In Japan, the state broadcaster NHK produced the world's first HD television system called MUSE, which started broadcasting in 1985. France followed shortly after with its HD MAC satellite broadcasts in 1984. These early systems utilized analog signals with 720p resolution, which laid the groundwork for the later digital HD systems that became standardized worldwide.

The first High Definition (HD) broadcasts on TV took place in the late 1970s in Switzerland, where a few experimental broadcasts were conducted using the analog MUSE system, developed by IBM. However, it wasn't until the United States showcased HD at the 1996 Summer Olympics in Atlanta that HD broadcasting began gaining momentum internationally. These broadcasts marked the transition towards the digital era, with HDTVs eventually becoming mainstream by the end of the 1990s.

The first High Definition (HD) broadcasts on TV began in the late 1990s. Japan was at the forefront, with NHK conducting experimental HD broadcasts as early as 1989, but regular HD broadcasting started in the U.S. in 1998 when the FCC approved the ATSC standard for digital television, which included HD formats. By 1999, several major networks and cable providers in the U.S. had launched their first HD channels.

The first high-definition television (HDTV) broadcasts took place in the United States in 1993 during the opening ceremony of the NBA All-Star Game. The event was transmitted using the ATSC (Advanced Television Systems Committee) format. This broadcast marked a significant milestone in television history as it marked the first time a live event was broadcast in high definition.
